books.title: AI Basics
books.tagline: Maths, not magic.
books.blurb: Follow Leo as he asks a chatbot what to cook for 4 friends, and see how AI learns, how it answers, who is behind it and what the rules are around the world.
gist: A chatbot runs on an LLM (large language model) that learned by guessing missing words.
It answers one word at a time, so it can sound sure and be wrong.
Give it details, keep secrets out, and check what matters.
pt: Fill in the blank, millions of times
Use it like a smart friend, not an oracle

books.title: When AI Gets It Wrong
books.tagline: Confident isn't correct.
books.blurb: Follow Mia as a chatbot helps with her honeybee report, invents a book, agrees too easily and tips a story one way, and learn how to check it like a detective.
gist: Chatbots can make up answers that sound true (hallucinations).
They can agree too easily and repeat old biases from their training data.
Open the source, ask how sure it is, and check a second place.

books.title: Using AI Yourself
books.tagline: The higher you climb, the more you check.
books.blurb: Tomas climbs from one homework question to a weekly study routine. Learn the ladders and the snakes of using a chatbot yourself.
gist: Chatbots can sound sure and still be wrong.
Let AI quiz you, not think for you.
Know what happens to your chats, and what to keep private.

books.title: Searching with AI
books.tagline: The summary is a starting card, not the book.
books.blurb: Elif asks if she can pack a power bank for a flight. See how AI search answers are built, where the ads go, and why the source still matters.
gist: AI answers are built from many searches and linked pages.
With an AI summary, people clicked fewer links.
Open the cited page and check the official source.

books.title: AI, Jobs & School
books.tagline: Use AI to think harder, not to skip the thinking.
books.blurb: Ines writes a final essay and applies for a weekend office job. See how AI is changing schoolwork, first jobs and the rules around both.
gist: Schools set their own AI rules; check yours.
AI tends to change the tasks in a job more than erase it.
Employers still want people who can explain their thinking.
pt: The office job, before and after

books.title: Deepfakes & Scams
books.tagline: Checking beats spotting.
books.blurb: Ravi gets a call that sounds just like his aunt. Spot the clues, see the scammer's playbook, and set up a simple family plan.
gist: AI can copy a voice or face from a short clip.
Rush, secrecy and odd payment methods are the biggest clues.
Hang up, call back on a known number, and use a family safe word.

books.title: Your Data, Privacy & Copyright
books.tagline: Your data, your art, your face.
books.blurb: Walk through Noor's first art show: what happens to what she types, whether her foxes trained an AI, who owns AI-made art, and the light on a visitor's smart glasses.
gist: Chats can train AI unless you switch it off.
Prompts alone don't make you an author; human work does.
Smart-glasses lights help, but asking is better.

books.title: AI and Your Health
books.tagline: Prepare with AI. Decide with a clinician.
books.blurb: Kofi asks a chatbot about a cough that won't go away. See what it can and can't do, how nurses and regulators use and check AI, and when to skip the chatbot entirely.
gist: Chatbots can explain, but they can't examine you.
In one study, people with chatbots decided no better than people without.
In an emergency, call your local emergency number.

books.title: AI Agents
books.tagline: A chatbot answers. An agent does.
books.blurb: Follow Zara, a student, as an AI agent books dinner for 8 on Saturday, seen from her side, the AI company's, the restaurant's, the bank's and the referees' around the world.
gist: An AI agent does the job (books the table), not just chats.
You pay by subscription, or ads pay for free plans, so ask whose side it is on.
When it slips up, the restaurant is the first stop, then the bank; keep the agent on a valet key.

books.title: How an AI Agent Is Built
books.tagline: A good agent is a short recipe with a human taster.
books.blurb: Omar builds an AI helper for his family's bike shop that handles one return, start to finish. See the ingredients, the rules and where a person stays in charge.
gist: An agent is a model with tools and instructions.
Give it only the access the job needs.
For money moves, a person should approve first.
pt: Should it pay out on its own?

books.title: When AI Does the Shopping
books.tagline: Always confirm the buy; keep the receipt.
books.blurb: Jonah lets an AI watch the price of rain boots and buy them for him. Then he gets charged twice. Who sells, who pays, and how you get your money back.
gist: A shopping agent can watch prices and buy only after you confirm.
The AI shops; the store still sells.
Keep your receipts and know your dispute window.

books.title: What Powers AI
books.tagline: One question is small; billions add up.
books.blurb: Hana asks an AI one question for her science fair. Follow it to a data centre and see the chips, electricity and water behind every answer.
gist: One AI question travels to a data centre where chips, electricity and cooling answer it.
One prompt is small; billions add up.
Look for figures with a date and a source.
pt: Most of it goes to the chips

books.title: Robots & Physical AI
books.tagline: Real robots are often boring arms.
books.blurb: Kai orders a water bottle and a robot arm called Rivet picks it. See how robots learn, what the makers say, and who keeps workers safe.
gist: Physical AI moves real things; a world model predicts what happens next.
Ask if a robot is a demo, a pilot or a product.
Workers and robots often share the job.

books.title: Open vs Closed AI
books.tagline: Read the licence; know where your data goes.
books.blurb: Rosa wants AI to help answer her bakery's emails. Should she download an open model or pay for a closed one? Compare cost, privacy, control and the rules.
gist: Open-weight models can be downloaded and run yourself; closed ones are used via an app or API.
Read the licence before you build on a model.
Know where your data goes.

books.title: Tokenization
books.tagline: Same fund, new receipt.
books.blurb: Amara has $1,000 saved and spots a tokenized fund in her app. Is it a new kind of money, or the same fund with a new receipt? Here's what changes and what doesn't.
gist: Tokenizing a fund changes how ownership is recorded, not what the fund holds.
Big firms like BlackRock, Franklin Templeton and DTCC are trying it, mostly for large investors so far.
A tokenized security is still a security: ask who keeps the record and who can fix mistakes.
pt: A digital twin in the vault

books.title: Why Your Mortgage Moves
books.tagline: Your rate rides the bond market, not just the Fed.
books.blurb: Diego is buying his first home. Why did his mortgage rate jump, when the Fed was cutting? Follow his rate from the bank to the bond market.
gist: A mortgage rate is set by investors in the bond market, not directly by the Fed.
Mortgage rates tend to move with the 10-year Treasury yield.
Get at least three written offers and compare the APR.
pt: Where the bank gets the money
A short dial, a long road

books.title: The Debt Loop
books.tagline: A second card paying the first. What could go wrong?
books.blurb: Why borrowing to pay interest feeds itself, told through one student's $20 a week.
gist: Borrowing to pay interest makes debt grow on itself: in 2026 about half of new US borrowing just covered interest.
When lots of borrowed money moves at once, a calm market can suddenly panic.
New money reaches some people before prices rise, and others after.

books.title: Dollar, Gold and Yen
books.tagline: Two rulers, one canary, and a trip to Japan.
books.blurb: Lucia is saving dollars for a trip to Japan. Why does her money buy more yen this year, why do central banks keep buying gold, and why do people watch the yen?
gist: A dollar can look strong against other money and still buy less at the shop.
Money tends to move toward higher interest rates, which moves exchange rates.
A sudden jump in the yen can be an early sign of market stress.

books.title: Two Schools of Economics
books.tagline: One closed factory, two readings, and a shared rooftop.
books.blurb: A factory closes and Grace's café goes quiet. Two schools of economics read the same slump in different ways. Hear both, then decide what you think.
gist: Keynesians focus on the slump: when spending falls, boost it, and ease off when things run hot.
Austrians look at the boom before: cheap credit can lead firms to build more than people want.
Both want steady prices and jobs; they differ on how, and real countries mix both.
pt: Sugar rush? The crash is the bill

books.title: Fintech Rails
books.tagline: Five roads for one $600 bike.
books.blurb: Felix buys a $600 bike from a small shop. The same money can travel five different roads: card, ACH, wire, instant transfer or stablecoin. Here's how fast each one is, what it costs, and which one has an undo.
gist: A card tap is approved in seconds, but the money follows later, in batches between banks.
Instant rails like RTP and FedNow move money in seconds, any day, but those payments are final.
Speed and safety pull in opposite directions: card buyers can dispute charges, instant payers usually can't.

books.title: Stablecoins
books.tagline: A $1 ticket that never sleeps.
books.blurb: Follow Ana's $100 as it becomes a digital dollar: what backs it, who earns the interest, the rules around the world, and what it means for you.
gist: A stablecoin is a digital claim ticket worth $1, backed mostly by short US government IOUs and cash.
The interest on that backing goes to the issuer and its partners; holders get none, by law in the US and EU.
It is fast and works 24/7, but it is not a bank account: no deposit insurance, and it can wobble below $1.

books.title: Why is everything so expensive?
books.tagline: Same cart. Bigger receipt. Bruh.
books.blurb: Why prices keep climbing, told through Sam's $100 Saturday shop.
gist: Inflation means the same money buys less: US prices roughly doubled since 2000.
The 2021-22 spike had several causes stacked together: money and demand, supply chains, energy and some company pricing.
Inflation quietly moves buying power between shoppers, savers, workers, borrowers and governments.
pt: Too much money, too few things

books.title: How Starlink Works
books.tagline: The cell tower moves to the sky.
books.blurb: Follow Ila, on a farm 40 km from town, as her data leaves a dish on the roof, hops to a moving satellite, lands at a ground station and joins the internet. Then see how her phone reaches space, how Starlink differs from its rivals, who pays, and where it is heading.
gist: Starlink beams internet from thousands of satellites flying about 480 km up, so homes far from cables can get online with a small dish.
Each satellite passes overhead in minutes; the dish hands off between them, and the data drops to ground stations wired to fiber.
Ordinary phones are next: texting via satellite works today, and fuller phone service is SpaceX's goal for around 2028.
pt: A phone that talks to space

books.title: How SpaceX Rockets Work
books.tagline: Land it, fly it again, fill it up.
books.blurb: Nia, a student with a cardboard rocket and a lot of questions, finds out why SpaceX lands its rockets, how a tower catches one with 'chopsticks', and why a gas station in orbit could get people back to the Moon.
gist: Rockets cost far more than their parts, and most are still thrown away after one flight.
SpaceX lands its boosters and catches its giant Super Heavy booster with a tower, so it can fly them again.
The twist: refilling in orbit. Estimates run from 6 to 22 launches, all made before NASA's Oct 23 route change.
pt: Rockets cost way more than their parts
